groups.rule: find — an ingestion helper that accepts a country code in any of its forms and answers with the alpha-3 identity, or "(none)". NOT what the wire uses: a country travels as its alpha-3 and nothing else, because three accepted forms would give one value three encodings. Leniency is safe here only because the forms occupy disjoint shapes — two letters, three letters, three digits — so nothing is guessed.

find — case is normalised, and this is the group with a real trap in it. C# must use ToUpperInvariant rather than ToUpper: under a Turkish locale "ie".ToUpper() is "İE", a dotted capital I, and Ireland stops resolving on machines in one country. JavaScript's toUpperCase is locale-independent by default, so the trap is one-sided — which is exactly why the normalisation is written deliberately in both rather than left to each caller.

cases.note: The dotted-I case. Ireland's alpha-2 is IE, so a culture-sensitive upper-casing turns this into "İE" and finds nothing — but only when the process runs under a Turkish locale.

groups.rule: find — no match. A code that names no row is an ordinary outcome when the value came from somewhere else, so it answers rather than throwing.

cases.note: Three characters but neither all-letters nor all-digits, so it matches no form.

groups.rule: properties — invariants that must hold for every input, so the expected value is "true" and comes from the rule rather than from any implementation.

cases.note: All three forms of one country find the same row. This is what makes accepting three forms a convenience rather than three different answers.
